prompt: A platform’s posting rate stays constant, but posts now reach many more eligible follower timelines. What changes with fan-out on write?

options.text: Only the canonical post write rate changes.
options.explanation: The number of posts is unchanged; the extra work is inserting references into recipient timelines.

options.text: No work changes because identifiers are smaller than post bodies.
options.explanation: Small entries still require an operation for each eligible recipient.

options.text: Every follower count can be replaced with the unweighted account average.
options.explanation: Posting frequency and recipient eligibility affect which follower counts matter.

options.text: Background timeline inserts increase, and concentrated large accounts can dominate backlog.
options.explanation: Correct. Fan-out amplifies each post by its eligible recipients; averages hide concentrated work.

workedExample: Count the recipient timelines each actual post updates. Measure both aggregate insert demand and the largest bursts. Separate that work from canonical post storage and foreground hydration; reducing bytes per entry does not remove write amplification.

link.title: System Design Primer: design the Twitter timeline

prompt: In a hypothetical feed, 400M posts produce 30B eligible timeline inserts per day: 75 per post. A naive calculation instead uses 200 followers per account. Which explanation could account for the difference?

options.text: Twitter only delivered every third tweet to save resources.
options.explanation: Wrong. The stated hypothetical workload does not establish sampling. The eligible-recipient count may instead differ from an unweighted follower average.

options.text: Follower counts are heavily skewed and many accounts post to few or inactive followers, and fan-out only writes to users who have a cached timeline.
options.explanation: Correct as a possible explanation: posting frequency weights the follower distribution, and eligibility/activity filters reduce deliveries. A skewed distribution alone does not prove that post-weighted fan-out is lower.

options.text: Each delivery covered several followers at once using Redis transactions.
options.explanation: Wrong. A delivery here is one insert into one timeline. Batching changes the number of network calls, not the number of deliveries.

options.text: The 30 billion figure counts only celebrity tweets.
options.explanation: Wrong. The prompt counts all eligible inserts, not just celebrity posts. It supplies no historical celebrity-only measurement.

workedExample: An account average gives equal weight to quiet and prolific authors. Fan-out instead weights each author by the posts they actually create and then filters recipient eligibility. Activity rules can reduce deliveries, while prolific high-follower authors can increase them. Measure eligible recipients per actual post; skew alone does not determine the direction.
